input:
Principle
Distillation is a separation technique that works by exploiting the difference in volatility between the components of a liquid mixture. When the mixture is heated to boiling, it produces a vapour that is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it leaves behind, and condensing that vapour produces a liquid with the same enriched composition. A single step of this kind changes the composition by only a limited amount, but the column repeats the step on a whole stack of contacting stages, so that the enrichment effectively compounds from stage to stage and the vapour leaving the top is far richer in the volatile component than the original feed. Meanwhile, the less volatile component concentrates in the descending liquid, and the column ultimately delivers an enriched overhead product together with a depleted bottoms product from a single feed.

The working picture that underlies all of this is the equilibrium stage. On any given stage, vapour rising from below and liquid flowing down from above are brought into intimate contact and are assumed to leave in equilibrium with each other, at the composition fixed by the equilibrium relation for the stage temperature. The liquid composition on a stage is denoted by $x$ and the vapour composition by $y$, stated for the more volatile component throughout, while the feed composition is denoted by $z$. An overall material balance over the column ties the products to the feed: the feed divides into overhead and bottoms, and the volatile component in the feed divides between them in exactly the same accounting. A balance taken over the top of the column, around the stages above the feed, gives the rectifying relation between the vapour rising from a stage and the liquid descending to it, and a balance over the bottom gives the stripping relation, which has the same form. Reflux, which is the part of the condensed overhead that is returned to the column, sets the liquid traffic in the rectifying part, and boil-up sets the vapour traffic in the stripping part. Taken together, the two relations and the equilibrium relation between them constitute the whole of the simple model: stage compositions follow by stepping from one product towards the other, alternating between the balance relation, which moves along the column, and the equilibrium relation, which crosses between the phases on a stage.

Equipment
In its industrial form, the column consists of a vertical shell fitted with either trays or packing, together with a reboiler at the base and a condenser at the top. Trays hold liquid right across the cross-section of the column and pass the rising vapour through it, in the familiar downcomer-and-weir arrangement that maintains a liquid level on each tray and provides the contact that the stage picture assumes. Packing, by contrast, fills the shell with a structured or dumped surface over which the liquid spreads out as a film while the vapour rises through the voids, and the packed height is rated in terms of the height that performs as one equilibrium stage. The reboiler boils the bottoms liquid in order to supply the rising vapour, in either a kettle or a thermosiphon circuit, and the condenser condenses the overhead vapour, returning part of it as reflux and drawing off the rest as product. A reflux drum collects the condensate and splits the two streams.

The feed enters at the stage whose composition most closely matches the feed itself, part-way up the shell, with the rectifying part above the entry point and the stripping part below it. The instruments fitted to the column include temperature readings along the shell, which track the composition profile because temperature and composition move together along the column, the pressure reading that fixes the equilibrium behaviour, and the level and flow controls that hold the material balance assumed in the design. Materials of construction are selected according to the corrosive character of the mixture and the temperatures prevailing at the two ends of the column, and the internals are chosen with regard to the fouling that the feed is expected to lay down.

Worked example
Let us take the feed described in the Principle part, with composition $z$ in the more volatile component, and follow the stepping construction using the relations stated there. We begin from the bottoms product. The bottoms liquid, with composition $x_B$, sits on the lowest stage; applying the equilibrium relation gives the vapour leaving that stage, enriched in the volatile component relative to $x_B$ by the amount that the equilibrium relation states at that composition. The stripping relation then gives the liquid descending onto the stage from the stage above it, and applying the equilibrium relation once again gives the vapour leaving that stage. In this way the composition climbs stage by stage: each crossing from liquid to vapour produces an enrichment, and each move along the stripping relation repositions the liquid ready for the next crossing.

At the feed stage, the accounting switches to the rectifying relation, because the liquid traffic above the feed carries the reflux rather than the feed-augmented flow found below it, and the stepping then continues on the rectifying relation towards the top of the column. The final crossing gives the vapour that the condenser receives, with composition $y_D$, and condensation without any change of composition yields the overhead product at that same composition. The number of crossings is the stage count that the separation requires under the simple model, and it can be read directly off the construction: the stepping stops as soon as the composition passes the overhead product composition, and the stage on which it passes is the last stage to be counted. The check on the whole construction is provided by the overall balance of the Principle part: the overhead and bottoms amounts obtained from the stepping must return the feed amount and the feed composition when they are combined, and a construction that fails to close the balance has misapplied a relation at some stage, most frequently at the feed stage where the relation changes.

Limits
It is important to recognise that the simple model fails wherever its stage picture fails. The model assumes that each stage actually reaches equilibrium, whereas a real tray leaves the vapour and the liquid short of equilibrium, and the shortfall varies with traffic, froth behaviour, and entrainment, so the stage count predicted by the model understates the number of trays that a real column needs by a margin that the model itself does not supply. The model also treats the equilibrium relation as though it were fixed by the mixture alone; mixtures whose components interact strongly bend the relation, and a mixture that forms an azeotrope possesses a composition at which the vapour and the liquid are completely identical, where no stepping construction can cross and ordinary distillation simply cannot pass. Heat losses from the shell, pressure drop through the internals, and variations in traffic where heats of mixing are large all lie outside the model as stated. Nevertheless, the model remains the working picture for what a column does and for the size of separation that a stated reflux can buy, and its numbers provide the starting point for a rating exercise that puts the real behaviour back in.

Heated to boiling, the mixture gives a vapour richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it leaves, and condensation of that vapour gives a liquid of the same enriched composition. One such step changes the composition by a limited amount; the column repeats the step on a stack of contacting stages, so that the enrichment compounds from stage to stage and the vapour leaving the top is far richer in the volatile component than the feed. The less volatile component concentrates in the liquid that descends, and the column delivers an enriched overhead product and a depleted bottoms product from a single feed.

On a stage, vapour rising from below and liquid flowing from above are brought into contact and are taken to leave in equilibrium with each other, at the composition the equilibrium relation fixes for the stage temperature. The enrichment on one stage is bounded by the equilibrium relation, and the bound is what makes the column a stack rather than a single vessel. Where the components differ widely in volatility, the enrichment per stage is large and few stages separate them; where the volatilities are close, each crossing gains little and the stage count grows, with the reflux growing with it, because a leaner enrichment must be compounded more times and the traffic that carries the compounding is the reflux and the boil-up. The feed state enters the same accounting: a feed already at its boiling point joins the traffic without disturbing it, while a cold feed draws heat from the traffic at the feed stage and a vaporised feed adds to the vapour rising from it.

A column run at higher reflux moves more material between the phases on every stage and pays for the movement in reboiler steam and condenser cooling in proportion. The equipment is therefore sized as a system — shell, trays or packing, reboiler, condenser, and drum together — and a change to any one item, a larger condenser or a different tray, moves the operating point of the rest.
